This year, the trees sprouted one of their best crops in decades, which prompted the baby boom.

Officials say 79 females nested this year, laying a total of 258 eggs. More than half of them never hatched. Some chicks that did emerge died soon after. Once the youngest chick reaches that point, conservationists confirm the official chick count.

Most of the chicks will get names when they turn a year old, in February and March of next year. However, experts plan to leave a handful of chicks unnamed—a sign of the species’ gradual transition toward a future with less human intervention.

With that goal in mind, conservationists also made some changes to the way they managed the birds this year. They used data from remote nest technology to keep tabs on the eggs and chicks, reducing the need for as many in-person checks. They also reduced supplementary feeding in some areas.
Fun fact: Dad of the year

Conservationists awarded “dad of the year” to Tūterangi, a 10-year-old male who bred for the first time. Despite being a first-time father, he mated with six females and produced ten living chicks, per RNZ.

Breeding populations live on three predator-free islands: Codfish, Anchor and Chalky. But after the record breeding season, the birds are running out of room. “If we want to keep kakapomaxxing, we need to fix the kakapo housing crisis,” environmental journalist Ellen Rykers tells the Spinoff’s Hayden Donnell.
Moving forward, conservationists say they need to create even more predator-free habitats for the parrots, with the eventual goal of returning kakapo to the island of Rakiura, their ancestral home.

Computer simulations suggest the next breeding season could occur in two years. So, while conservationists are taking a moment to celebrate the species’ recent gains, they’re “already looking ahead to 2028 and preparing for what could come next,” Vercoe says in the statement.
